extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and assessing the grounds, handling, and consequences of a journal retraction and related research-integrity concerns in published work. Focuses on what justifies retraction, editorial procedures, authorship responsibility, and record-keeping/replication practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction grounds: data do not support reported findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction issued when an internal examination 'found that the data do not support the reported findings. We therefore are retracting this article.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal institutional finding that the underlying data fail to support the paper's reported conclusions is presented as a clear ground for retraction; the retraction statement itself may be the primary public record of that finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and specificity of retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors noted it is unusual not to be told what specific errors were made; 'The data not supporting the findings is ambiguous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices that lack specific details about the errors or misconduct create ambiguity and hinder the community's ability to assess what conclusions remain trustworthy. Best practice is to provide as much clear context as permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial handling of submissions by associate editors and board members
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy described: 'papers from editorial board members are handled in exactly the same way as regular submissions... The only difference is that I handle all manuscripts by associate editors... they are 'blinded' within the system so that he/she cannot find out who is reviewing his/her paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should avoid special privileges for editors as authors: ensure independent handling, blinding of author identity within the review system, and direct handling by a separate editor to prevent suggestion of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-author due diligence and shared responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-author Gary Marcus: 'I never actually saw the raw data, just his summaries, so I can’t speak to the exact nature of what went wrong.' Commenters: 'You’re on the paper, you’re responsible for its contents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-authors bear responsibility for the paper; relying solely on summarized data from a colleague leaves co-authors unable to vouch for results. Reasonable due diligence may include reviewing primary/raw data or having clearly documented roles and verification steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete raw data and record-keeping (video records, field notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replication discovered 'the video records and field notes collected ... are incomplete for two of the conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain complete, auditable raw records (e.g., full video recordings and contemporaneous field notes). Incomplete records undermine the integrity and reproducibility of reported findings and can trigger re-examination or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication and re-running experiments when records are problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Following discovery of incomplete records, authors 'returned ... to re-run the three main experimental conditions ... videotaping every trial and accompanying the video records with field notes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When original records are insufficient, robust replication with thorough documentation (e.g., complete videotaping and detailed field notes) is an appropriate remedial step to verify reported results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal-level investigation triggered by institutional findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Science indicated it 'will also look into a 2007 paper ... after reviewing Harvard’s investigation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional investigations can prompt journals to conduct their own reviews of earlier publications, potentially leading to editorial actions (expressions of concern, corrections, or retractions). Journals should follow up on credible institutional findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of retractions on trust and citation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote: 'This retraction creates a quandary ... about whether other results are to be trusted as well... If scientists can’t trust published papers, the whole process breaks down.' The post also notes how often the paper had been cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions can undermine confidence in related literature; tracking citation counts of retracted papers and clearly communicating the scope of the problem helps the field assess downstream impacts and correct the citation record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acceptance of responsibility by authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction text includes the sentence: 'MH accepts responsibility for the error.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author acknowledgement of responsibility is often included in retraction notices; while important symbolically, such statements should be accompanied by factual detail about the nature of the error or misconduct where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship transparency: contribution statements to clarify who did what
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters suggested 'journals may need to require coauthors to outline who did what for the paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring explicit author contribution statements can clarify responsibilities, reduce exploitation of junior researchers, and help determine culpability when problems are discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of abusive practices: adding respected coauthors to mask problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary: 'If you like to cook your data, you want to have as many respected names as possible on your papers. Makes your pattern of “findings” less suspicious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to the anti-pattern where fraudulent or questionable work is 'laundered' through the inclusion of high-profile coauthors; editorial and institutional safeguards (contribution disclosure, data availability requirements) can mitigate this risk.
